pool_metadata.subject: English
pool_metadata.note: Original Cambridge-style questions. Not actual Cambridge content.

questions.stem: I ______ to the new science museum last weekend.
questions.explanation: Past simple is used for completed actions at a specific past time ('last weekend').

questions.stem: She ______ three novels since the beginning of the year.
questions.explanation: Present perfect is used for actions that started in the past and continue to the present ('since the beginning of the year').

questions.stem: We ______ in this neighbourhood for over ten years now.
questions.explanation: Present perfect with 'for' indicates duration from past to present.

questions.stem: While Tariq ______ his homework, the lights went out.
questions.explanation: Past continuous is used for an action in progress when interrupted by another past event.

questions.stem: Look at those dark clouds — it ______ any minute now.
questions.explanation: 'Going to' is used for predictions based on present evidence (dark clouds).

questions.stem: The concert ______ at 7:30 tomorrow evening.
questions.explanation: Present simple is used for scheduled/timetabled future events.

questions.stem: If you ______ harder, you will pass the test easily.
questions.explanation: First conditional uses present simple in the if-clause and will + infinitive in the main clause.

questions.stem: If I ______ enough money, I would travel around Asia.
questions.explanation: Second conditional uses past simple in the if-clause to describe unreal/hypothetical present situations.

questions.stem: The new library ______ by the mayor next Friday.
questions.explanation: Future passive: will + be + past participle. The library receives the action.

questions.stem: This bridge ______ over two hundred years ago.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle.

questions.stem: 'I am feeling tired,' said Amira. — Amira said that she ______ tired.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present continuous changes to past continuous.

questions.stem: 'We will finish the project tomorrow,' the students said. — The students said they ______ the project the next day.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, 'will' changes to 'would' and 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day'.

questions.stem: That is the artist ______ paintings were displayed at the gallery.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' is used as a possessive relative pronoun (the artist's paintings).

questions.stem: The documentary, ______ was released last month, has won several awards.
questions.explanation: In non-defining relative clauses (with commas), 'which' is used for things, not 'that'.

questions.stem: You ______ wear a helmet when riding a bicycle. It's the law.
questions.explanation: 'Must' expresses obligation/legal requirement.

questions.stem: He ______ be at work — I just saw him at the shopping centre.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' is used for logical deduction when something is impossible based on evidence.

questions.stem: Nadia suggested ______ to the botanical garden for our class trip.
questions.explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by a gerund (-ing form).

questions.stem: The teacher reminded the students ______ their permission slips.
questions.explanation: 'Remind someone' is followed by 'to + infinitive'.

questions.stem: This is ______ film I have ever watched.
questions.explanation: Superlative form with 'the most' + long adjective after 'the ... I have ever'.

questions.stem: My brother is ______ engineer. He works at ______ oil company in Abu Dhabi.
questions.explanation: 'An' before vowel sound ('engineer'). 'The' for a specific, known company.

questions.stem: By the time we arrived at the stadium, the match ______ (already / start).
questions.explanation: Past perfect is used for an action completed before another past action.

questions.stem: Right now, the scientists ______ (conduct) experiments in the laboratory.
questions.explanation: Present continuous for actions happening at the moment of speaking ('right now').

questions.stem: Water ______ (boil) at 100 degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: Present simple for scientific facts and general truths.

questions.stem: This time next week, I ______ (fly) to Istanbul for the holidays.
questions.explanation: Future continuous for an action that will be in progress at a specific future time.

questions.stem: Over fifty languages ______ (speak) in this country.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive for general facts.

questions.stem: The suspect ______ (question) by detectives for over three hours before he confessed.
questions.explanation: Past perfect passive: had + been + past participle, for a passive action before another past event.

questions.stem: If she ______ (not / miss) the bus, she would have arrived on time.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: if + past perfect for unreal past situations.

questions.stem: I really enjoy ______ (listen) to podcasts about wildlife.
questions.explanation: 'Enjoy' is always followed by a gerund.

questions.stem: She has been interested ______ marine biology since she was a child.
questions.explanation: 'Interested in' is a fixed prepositional phrase.

questions.stem: The village is famous ______ its handmade pottery.
questions.explanation: 'Famous for' is a fixed collocation.

questions.stem: Each of the players were given a trophy after the final match.
questions.corrected_sentence: Each of the players was given a trophy after the final match.
questions.explanation: 'Each of' takes a singular verb.

questions.stem: I have went to that restaurant many times before.
questions.corrected_sentence: I have been to that restaurant many times before.
questions.explanation: Present perfect of 'go' (for visiting) is 'have been', not 'have went'.

questions.stem: This puzzle is more easier than the one we did yesterday.
questions.corrected_sentence: This puzzle is easier than the one we did yesterday.
questions.explanation: Short adjectives use -er for comparatives, not 'more + -er'.

questions.stem: She wants to become the doctor when she grows up.
questions.corrected_sentence: She wants to become a doctor when she grows up.
questions.explanation: Use 'a' when talking about a profession in general, not a specific one.

questions.stem: The coach told us that we should practise more harder if we want to win.
questions.corrected_sentence: The coach told us that we should practise harder if we wanted to win.
questions.explanation: Double comparative error: 'harder' already is comparative. Also 'want' should shift to 'wanted' in reported speech.

questions.stem: We arrived to the airport just in time for our flight.
questions.corrected_sentence: We arrived at the airport just in time for our flight.
questions.explanation: 'Arrive at' is used for specific locations (buildings, places). 'Arrive in' for cities/countries.

questions.stem: If I would know the answer, I would tell you immediately.
questions.corrected_sentence: If I knew the answer, I would tell you immediately.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: 'If + past simple', not 'If + would'.

questions.stem: Yesterday, Khalid goes to the market and bought some fresh vegetables.
questions.corrected_sentence: Yesterday, Khalid went to the market and bought some fresh vegetables.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' signals past tense. Both verbs must be in past simple.

questions.stem: Students must to wear their school uniform every day.
questions.corrected_sentence: Students must wear their school uniform every day.
questions.explanation: Modal verbs are followed directly by the base form, never 'to + infinitive'.

questions.stem: The scientist which discovered the new species received a prestigious award.
questions.corrected_sentence: The scientist who discovered the new species received a prestigious award.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is used for people. 'Which' is used for things.

questions.stem: Somebody broke the window during the storm.
questions.correct_answer: The window was broken during the storm.
questions.explanation: Active to passive transformation. Object becomes subject, verb becomes 'was + past participle'.

questions.stem: 'I will call you tomorrow,' Omar told Fatima.
questions.correct_answer: Omar told Fatima that he would call her the next day.
questions.explanation: Direct to reported speech: 'will' → 'would', 'you' → 'her', 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'.

questions.stem: I don't have a car, so I can't drive to work.
questions.correct_answer: If I had a car, I could drive to work.
questions.explanation: Rewriting a present fact as a second conditional hypothetical situation.

questions.stem: No other mountain in Africa is as tall as Kilimanjaro.
questions.correct_answer: Kilimanjaro is the tallest mountain in Africa.
questions.explanation: 'No other X is as ... as Y' = 'Y is the most/...est X'.

questions.stem: The water is too cold to swim in.
questions.correct_answer: The water is not warm enough to swim in.
questions.explanation: 'Too cold to ...' = 'not warm enough to ...'.

questions.stem: When he was younger, he played football every weekend.
questions.correct_answer: He used to play football every weekend when he was younger.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' for past habits or states that no longer apply.

questions.stem: The restaurant has excellent food. We went there last Friday.
questions.correct_answer: The restaurant where we went last Friday has excellent food.
questions.explanation: Combining two sentences using the relative adverb 'where'.

questions.stem: She started learning Arabic five years ago. She is still learning it.
questions.correct_answer: She has been learning Arabic for five years.
questions.explanation: Combining 'started in the past + still happening' into present perfect continuous with 'for'.

questions.stem: I'm sure that Layla is at the library right now.
questions.correct_answer: Layla must be at the library right now.
questions.explanation: 'Must + be' for strong deduction about the present.

questions.stem: A mechanic serviced my father's car last week.
questions.correct_answer: My father had his car serviced last week.
questions.explanation: Causative 'have something done': Subject + had + object + past participle.

questions.stem: The sunset over the harbour was absolutely ______. (BEAUTY)
questions.explanation: Noun 'beauty' → adjective 'beautiful' using suffix '-ful'.

questions.stem: The ______ of the ancient palace took over ten years. (CONSTRUCT)
questions.explanation: Verb 'construct' → noun 'construction' using suffix '-ion'.

questions.stem: Please handle the equipment ______. (CARE)
questions.explanation: Noun 'care' → adjective 'careful' → adverb 'carefully'.

questions.stem: It is ______ to use your phone during the examination. (LEGAL)
questions.explanation: Adjective 'legal' → negative 'illegal' using prefix 'il-'.

questions.stem: The ______ between the two teams was very intense. (COMPETE)
questions.explanation: Verb 'compete' → noun 'competition'.

questions.stem: The documentary about coral reefs was very ______. (INFORM)
questions.explanation: Verb 'inform' → adjective 'informative' using suffix '-ative'.

questions.stem: There has been a significant ______ in technology over the past decade. (IMPROVE)
questions.explanation: Verb 'improve' → noun 'improvement' using suffix '-ment'.

questions.stem: Unfortunately, the driver was quite ______ and caused an accident. (CARE)
questions.explanation: Noun 'care' → negative adjective 'careless' using suffix '-less'.

questions.stem: My uncle is a talented ______. He plays the violin in an orchestra. (MUSIC)
questions.explanation: Noun 'music' → person noun 'musician' using suffix '-ian'.

questions.stem: The children were very ______ about the upcoming school trip. (ENTHUSIASM)
questions.explanation: Noun 'enthusiasm' → adjective 'enthusiastic'.

questions.stem: It was ______ honour to meet the author of my favourite book.
questions.explanation: 'An' before a silent 'h' in 'honour' (vowel sound).

questions.stem: We stayed indoors ______ it was raining heavily outside.
questions.explanation: 'Because' introduces a reason clause.

questions.stem: The old castle was built ______ top of a steep hill.
questions.explanation: 'On top of' is a fixed prepositional phrase meaning 'at the highest point of'.

questions.stem: There are ______ of interesting activities to do in this city.
questions.explanation: 'Plenty of' means 'a lot of / more than enough'.

questions.stem: The twins look so similar that I can hardly tell ______ apart.
questions.explanation: Object pronoun 'them' after the verb 'tell'.

questions.stem: ______ the heavy traffic, we managed to reach the station on time.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' + noun phrase to express contrast.

questions.stem: She doesn't like spicy food and neither ______ her brother.
questions.explanation: 'Neither + auxiliary + subject' for agreeing with a negative statement.

questions.stem: Could you look ______ my cat while I am on holiday?
questions.explanation: 'Look after' means to take care of.

questions.stem: You haven't finished your homework yet, ______ you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement → positive question tag. 'haven't' → 'have'.

questions.stem: Do you remember the day ______ we first met?
questions.explanation: 'When' is used as a relative adverb for time.

questions.stem: The government plans to ______ a new law to protect endangered species.
questions.explanation: 'Introduce a law' is the correct collocation for bringing a new law into effect.

questions.stem: The explorers had to ______ many difficulties during their expedition.
questions.explanation: 'Overcome difficulties' means to succeed in dealing with problems.

questions.stem: The company had to ______ several employees due to financial problems.
questions.explanation: 'Sack' means to dismiss from employment. 'Resign' means to leave voluntarily.

questions.stem: The hotel offers ______ views of the mountains from every room.
questions.explanation: 'Spectacular views' means impressively beautiful or grand.

questions.stem: We need to ______ a solution before the deadline.
questions.explanation: 'Come up with' means to think of or produce an idea or solution.

questions.stem: I accidentally ______ an old photograph while tidying my room.
questions.explanation: 'Come across' means to find something by chance.

questions.stem: Could you ______ me a favour and help me carry these boxes?
questions.explanation: 'Do someone a favour' is a fixed collocation.

questions.stem: Let's ______ a decision before it's too late.
questions.explanation: 'Make a decision' is a fixed collocation.

questions.passage: Urban farming is becoming increasingly popular in cities around the world. People are transforming rooftops, balconies, and abandoned lots into productive green spaces. These urban farms not only provide fresh produce for local communities but also help reduce carbon emissions by cutting down on food transportation. In Singapore, for example, vertical farms now supply over 10% of the country's leafy vegetables. Critics argue that urban farming cannot replace traditional agriculture, but supporters believe it is an important part of creating more sustainable cities.
questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To explain the benefits and growth of urban farming
To describe farming techniques in Singapore only
To argue that urban farming should replace all other agriculture
questions.correct_answer: To explain the benefits and growth of urban farming
questions.explanation: The passage discusses urban farming's popularity, benefits, and examples — the main purpose is to explain and inform.

questions.passage: Urban farming is becoming increasingly popular in cities around the world. People are transforming rooftops, balconies, and abandoned lots into productive green spaces. These urban farms not only provide fresh produce for local communities but also help reduce carbon emissions by cutting down on food transportation. In Singapore, for example, vertical farms now supply over 10% of the country's leafy vegetables. Critics argue that urban farming cannot replace traditional agriculture, but supporters believe it is an important part of creating more sustainable cities.
questions.stem: According to the passage, what percentage of leafy vegetables do Singapore's vertical farms supply?
questions.explanation: The passage states 'vertical farms now supply over 10% of the country's leafy vegetables'.

questions.passage: Urban farming is becoming increasingly popular in cities around the world. People are transforming rooftops, balconies, and abandoned lots into productive green spaces. These urban farms not only provide fresh produce for local communities but also help reduce carbon emissions by cutting down on food transportation. In Singapore, for example, vertical farms now supply over 10% of the country's leafy vegetables. Critics argue that urban farming cannot replace traditional agriculture, but supporters believe it is an important part of creating more sustainable cities.
questions.stem: What can be inferred about the critics mentioned in the passage?
options: They think urban farming is completely useless
They believe urban farming has limitations in scale
They want to ban urban farming
They have never seen an urban farm
questions.correct_answer: They believe urban farming has limitations in scale
questions.explanation: Critics say it 'cannot replace traditional agriculture' — implying they see it as limited, not sufficient on its own.

questions.passage: The discovery of penicillin in 1928 revolutionised medicine. Before antibiotics, even minor infections could be fatal. Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould growing on a petri dish had destroyed the bacteria around it. This accidental observation led to the development of the first antibiotic. However, today scientists warn that the overuse of antibiotics is creating drug-resistant bacteria, which could undo decades of medical progress.
questions.stem: In the passage, the word 'fatal' is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: 'Fatal' means causing death.

questions.passage: The discovery of penicillin in 1928 revolutionised medicine. Before antibiotics, even minor infections could be fatal. Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould growing on a petri dish had destroyed the bacteria around it. This accidental observation led to the development of the first antibiotic. However, today scientists warn that the overuse of antibiotics is creating drug-resistant bacteria, which could undo decades of medical progress.
questions.stem: How did Fleming discover penicillin?
options: He noticed mould had killed bacteria by accident
Another scientist told him about it
He read about it in a medical journal
questions.correct_answer: He noticed mould had killed bacteria by accident
questions.explanation: The passage calls it an 'accidental observation' — he noticed mould had destroyed bacteria.

questions.passage: The discovery of penicillin in 1928 revolutionised medicine. Before antibiotics, even minor infections could be fatal. Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould growing on a petri dish had destroyed the bacteria around it. This accidental observation led to the development of the first antibiotic. However, today scientists warn that the overuse of antibiotics is creating drug-resistant bacteria, which could undo decades of medical progress.
questions.stem: What does the author imply by saying antibiotic resistance could 'undo decades of medical progress'?
options: New diseases will appear from nowhere
Infections that are now treatable could become dangerous again
questions.correct_answer: Infections that are now treatable could become dangerous again
questions.explanation: If bacteria resist antibiotics, infections we can currently treat would become untreatable — returning to pre-antibiotic conditions.

questions.stem: I wish I ______ more time to finish the painting.
questions.explanation: 'Wish + past simple' for present wishes about unreal situations.

questions.stem: It was ______ a difficult question that nobody could answer it.
questions.explanation: 'Such + a/an + adjective + noun + that' is the correct pattern. 'So + adjective + that'.

questions.stem: Your hands are covered in paint! ______ you been painting all morning?
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous ('Have you been painting') for an action that started in the past with visible present results.

questions.stem: Neither Rami ______ Sara was able to attend the meeting.
questions.explanation: 'Neither ... nor' is a correlative conjunction pair.

questions.stem: The teacher asked us where we ______ (go) during the summer holidays.
questions.explanation: Reported question with past reference: 'did you go' → 'where we had gone'.

questions.stem: If only I ______ (study) harder for the exam. I failed by just two marks.
questions.explanation: 'If only / wish + past perfect' for regrets about the past.

questions.stem: You ______ (should / tell) me earlier. Now it's too late to change anything.
questions.explanation: 'Should have + past participle' for past actions that were advisable but didn't happen.

questions.stem: The town ______ I grew up has changed completely.
questions.explanation: 'Where' is used as a relative adverb for places.

questions.stem: It's a pity I can't play a musical instrument.
questions.correct_answer: I wish I could play a musical instrument.
questions.explanation: 'Wish + could' for abilities we don't have but want.

questions.stem: Although the weather was terrible, we enjoyed the picnic.
questions.correct_answer: Despite the terrible weather, we enjoyed the picnic.
questions.explanation: 'Although + clause' → 'Despite + noun phrase'.

questions.stem: She set an alarm because she didn't want to be late.
questions.correct_answer: She set an alarm in order not to be late.
questions.explanation: 'Because she didn't want to' → 'in order not to' for expressing negative purpose.

questions.stem: Someone delivers fresh flowers to the hotel every morning.
questions.correct_answer: The hotel has fresh flowers delivered every morning.
questions.explanation: Causative structure: 'have + object + past participle' when someone else performs the action.
